# Adapting the Experts to the Kind of Project

<!-- Generated by tools/build_lite.py from the full skill. Edit the source in skills/enterprise-experts/, then rebuild. -->

The expert reference sections are written with a hosted application in mind (a service with users, a database and deployments). Many projects are something else. Read the block that matches the project and use it in place of the service-shaped checks. The mission and the deliverable of each expert stay the same; the checks change.

If the capability matrix and your reading of the code disagree about what the project is, say so and ask the user.

## A tool, library, CLI, SDK or skill (installed and run by others; nothing hosted)

| # | Area | What to assess instead |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Security | What the tool executes and writes on the user's machine; injection through its inputs (file names, config, repository content); whether its guardrails can be bypassed; integrity of what it outputs (can a result be forged?); secrets it reads or logs; supply chain (dependencies, install scripts, pinned versions). Treat the tool's own user, and the content it processes, as possible attackers. |
| 3 | Performance | Run time and memory against input size, measured by timing at least five runs; start-up time; behaviour on a large input. |
| 4 | Scalability | Growth with input size (10×, 100×); many invocations at once on the same files (run them in parallel and look for lost or corrupted output); limits that are hit silently. |
| 5 | Reliability | Malformed, empty, huge and hostile input; interruption half-way (is state left consistent?); concurrent writers; clear failure instead of wrong output. Exit codes and error messages are its "health". |
| 6 | Database | Usually not applicable. On-disk formats and schemas the tool reads or writes belong to APIs (15). |
| 7 | Disaster Recovery | Usually not applicable: the asset is the source repository. Check that releases can be rebuilt from a tag and that nothing important exists only on one machine. |
| 8 | Observability | The user's ability to see what happened: exit codes, error messages, a verbose or debug mode, logs. Not dashboards. |
| 10 | DevOps | Release and distribution: version consistency across files, tags, a reproducible build of the artifact, checksums, a changelog, a tested install and upgrade path, CI on the supported platforms. |
| 11 | Infrastructure | Only the packaging the tool ships (a container image, a compose file): non-root user, read-only mounts, no socket or secrets, resource limits. Otherwise not applicable. |
| 12 | Cost | The cost it imposes on its users: time, compute, tokens or paid API calls per run. |
| 13 | UI/UX | The command-line or API experience: help text, argument names, defaults, error messages that say what to do, output that can be piped; and any report or page it generates. Do not mark not applicable just because there is no graphical interface. |
| 14 | Data Governance | What the tool reads, writes and sends anywhere; where its output lives; whether personal or secret data can end up in its output. |
| 15 | APIs | The public surface: commands and flags, exit codes, file formats and their versioning, a library's exported functions; compatibility promises between versions. |
| 18 | Incidents | How a bad release is handled: vulnerability reporting route, withdrawing or superseding a release, telling users. |
| 19 | Compliance | **Licensing first**: is there a licence, is it compatible with the dependencies' licences and with how the tool is distributed? A public repository without a licence gives nobody the right to use it. Then export, privacy or sector rules only if the tool handles such data. |
| 20 | Analytics | Usually not applicable; an offline tool should not phone home. If it has telemetry, check consent and what is sent. |

## A mobile app

Add to the usual checks: permissions requested versus used; secrets inside the app bundle; certificate handling; offline behaviour and sync conflicts; store requirements and privacy labels; build signing and release tracks; crash reporting; behaviour on small screens, with large text, and right-to-left.

## Infrastructure-only repository

Security, DevOps and Infrastructure carry the review: least privilege, exposure to the internet, state files and their secrets, drift, plan-before-apply in CI, module pinning, tagging and cost visibility. QA means validation, linting and policy checks. Business Logic and UI/UX are not applicable.

## Data pipeline or analytics project

Database and Data Governance carry the review: schemas and contracts between stages, idempotent and restartable runs, late and duplicate data, lineage, data quality checks with thresholds, backfills, personal data in intermediate storage, cost per run.

## A prototype or something not built yet

Say plainly what exists and what does not. When the code does not contain what the user described (a dependency is declared but nothing uses it, a journey has no code), that is the main finding: ask whether the code is elsewhere or unwritten. Findings about a design that is not built are requirements, rated for the exposure it will have, and labelled as such. The engine's decision for a prototype measures distance to release; say "there is nothing to release yet" rather than letting NO-GO read as an alarm.

## Reviewer-written checks (probes)

When no existing command shows what you need (an injection attempt, a concurrency test, a measurement), write a small script, run it and record the command, its exit code and its output in the evidence log.

- Keep probes in `<review>/probes/`. Never add them to the project, and make them work on copies or temporary folders so they cannot change the project.
- A probe that exits 0 only when the behaviour is correct can back a pass; one that demonstrates a defect should exit non-zero and backs the finding.
- For a finding discovered by reading, write the probe before the fix so the same probe can verify it afterwards.
- A probe proves what it tests and nothing more. An area whose only runs are your own probes is "Verified" in the scorecard's narrow sense; say in the deliverable what was and was not exercised.
- A check that cannot run because a dependency is missing may use a stand-in (a fake database client, for example); say so in the evidence title.
